proposal: The Mandate says PEPFAR and the President's Malaria Initiative should become part of an integrated, sustainable health network and transition smoothly to national ownership and funding, with better coordination between USAID's health programs and those initiatives. It also calls for focusing global health aid on outcomes rather than inputs, applying PEPFAR's data reforms to all global health programs, extending PEPFAR's shift toward local entities to all global health aid, and ramping down partnerships with UN agencies, international NGOs and large contractors.
remaining: Completing agreements and implementation plans in the roughly 71 countries in negotiation; Ghana and Zimbabwe declined, and Kenya's agreement faced legal challenges over data privacy before approval (Bush Center).
PEPFAR's statutory future: the short-term authorization expired in March 2025 and no reauthorization was found.

Mandate-specific reforms not verified: applying PEPFAR's data reforms to all global health programs, the integrated family-focused funding approach (p. 265), and an explicit ramp-down of partnerships with UN agencies, international NGOs and large contractors (p. 277).

status_summary: The State Department released the America First Global Health Strategy on 2025-09-18; the Bush Institute describes it as replacing large awards to US-based implementing partners with direct agreements with host-country governments that require governments to contribute more of their own money, and as moving PEPFAR toward country ownership by 2030 (State's own copy of the strategy could not be fetched). State Delegation of Authority No. 597 (published 2025-09-05) had already placed the global HIV/AIDS and global health security offices' authorities under an Under Secretary for Foreign Assistance. The first bilateral agreement, with Kenya, was signed on 2025-12-04 by Secretary Rubio and Kenya's Foreign Affairs Cabinet Secretary; its text, a copy hosted by Public Citizen, describes a five-year cooperation framework that disclaims status as a binding international agreement and any legal rights or obligations, and sets a goal of handing all U.S.-supported activities over to Kenya within five years. Planned US support falls from about $414 million in 2026 to about $161 million in 2030 (about $1.63 billion in total), while the planned rise in Kenyan domestic health spending above its 2025 baseline goes from none in 2026 to 10 billion shillings in 2027 and 50 billion in 2030; US funding of laboratory commodities declines from 2026 and ends after 2028, US funding of frontline health workers ends after 2027 with Kenya funding from 2028, and the US may reduce or end funding if co-investment falls short. A Bush Center update dated 2026-07-29 reported State officials saying 34 memoranda of understanding were complete and 71 countries were developing implementation plans, and on 2026-09-29 the Ghana News Agency quoted the US charge d'affaires in Accra saying State had signed 35 bilateral health memoranda (24 in sub-Saharan Africa) covering about $24.6 billion in new health funding, of which about $14.5 billion is US assistance and $10.1 billion recipient co-investment. The KFF tracker (data as of 2026-09-11) counts 35 agreements, mostly five-year plans for 2026 to 2030, with a stated $24.2 billion total, 39 percent from partner countries, and US funding down $7.4 billion (34 percent) against historical levels for those countries. Ghana's president rejected the proposed compact, and the Bush Center update reports that faith-based groups urged the White House budget office to release appropriated funds for PEPFAR (citing about $6 billion), the Global Fund and Gavi. The direction matches the Mandate's call for national ownership and co-financing, but the design differs: State-led bilateral compacts rather than a reformed USAID Global Health Bureau, with design choices (such as government-to-government agreements and data-sharing terms) that the Mandate did not specify.

timeline.event: Month-level date: PEPFAR's short-term authorization expires in March 2025, according to Aidspan, which describes an ongoing debate over the program's future structure.

State publishes Delegation of Authority No. 597 (signed 2025-08-21), moving the powers of the heads of its global HIV/AIDS and global health security offices, among others, to the Under Secretary for Foreign Assistance, Humanitarian Affairs, and Religious Freedom.

State releases the America First Global Health Strategy: direct agreements with host-country governments in place of large US-implementer awards, higher government contributions, collaboration with faith-based organizations, a shift of PEPFAR toward country ownership by 2030, and a goal of agreements with the largest recipients by March 2026 (per the Bush Institute's summary).

The US and Kenya sign a health cooperation framework at Washington under the strategy; the document disclaims status as a binding international agreement. Planned US support falls from about $414 million in 2026 to about $161 million in 2030 while the planned rise in Kenyan domestic health spending grows from none in 2026 to 50 billion shillings in 2030, with a goal of handing over all US-supported activities within five years and dated milestones (for example frontline laboratory workers on Kenya's payroll in 2028 and laboratory commodities fully Kenyan-funded by the end of the framework).

title: Move PEPFAR and global health aid toward country ownership and co-financing
uncertainties: State's own strategy document could not be read (state.gov returned HTTP 403), so the strategy's content comes from the Bush Institute and Aidspan summaries. The Kenya framework text was read through a browser retrieval supplied to the project and opened directly by the independent reviewer, who confirmed the signing date and signers, the legal-status clause, the five-year transition goal, the Appendix 1 funding schedule, the end of US frontline health worker funding after 2027 and the clause (para. 6.1) allowing the US to reduce or end funding if co-investment falls short. The retrieval describes US laboratory commodity funding as 100 percent in 2026, while the laboratory commodity table read by the reviewer shows a small existing Kenyan share in 2026, so the record says only that US funding declines and ends after 2028. The copy is hosted by Public Citizen, an advocacy organization; that it was released under a records request is an inference from the file name, not stated in the document. Other countries' texts, which Public Citizen's page links, were not read, so terms for them (for example the three-year agreements the KFF tracker lists for Bolivia, Botswana, Panama and South Sudan) were not checked. The MOU counts (34 on 2026-07-29, 35 on 2026-09-11 and 2026-09-29) and funding totals ($24.6 billion per the Ghana News Agency, $24.2 billion per KFF) differ slightly by source and date. The KFF and Public Citizen pages are trackers or advocacy compilations; the agreements themselves are the primary documents. The Aidspan article shows no date, so 2025-10-01 is an approximate month-level date for the source, and the PEPFAR authorization expiry date within March 2025 was not given and was not checked against a primary source. Funding disruptions and their causes are reported by advocacy groups and were not independently verified. The USAID Global Health Bureau the Mandate addresses no longer operates in its former form (see c09-01). The localization element is also tracked in c09-05. No PEPFAR reauthorization search was run.
